blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en:
. Generative retrieval trains a language model to generate the identifier
of a relevant document. Recent work replaces the autoregressive decoder
with diffusion, but changes identifiers, training recipe and decoding
at once, so differences cannot be credited to the paradigm. On NQ320K and MS300K, we train autoregressive,
masked-diffusion and block-diffusion models with residual-quantised,
product-quantised and random identifiers. With identifier length and
training budget fixed, we decode each model in several ways.
Decoding alone moves a diffusion model’s Hit@1 by 6.6 to 13.7 points. Our reference diffusion decoding, generate-and-match, generates an identifier, then retrieves the closest corpus
identifiers. The generated identifier is right for 14–21% of NQ320K queries. We test one-pass scoring to decode diffusion retrievers: the model
reads a fully masked identifier once, and each document is scored by its
codes’ probabilities. It matches or beats generate-and-match in 11 of 12 settings.
Autoregressive models still lead in Hit@1; on NQ320K, the lead comes from the model, not beam search. Starting from one
sampled identifier, one-pass scoring removes 46–83% of masked diffusion’s
deficit to beam search; from generate-and-match, at most a quarter. On NQ320K, every paradigm largely memorises which
identifier answers which query: random identifiers keep 83–90% of the Hit@1 of residual-quantised ones. There, product-quantised identifiers lead
residual-quantised ones by 3.4 points in the autoregressive model and by − 0.7 -0.7 to + 3.6 +3.6 in diffusion models; across decodings, AR’s gap exceeds diffusion’s by 1.5–2.3 points, around our ± 2 \pm 2 -point threshold. Paradigm comparisons must report each paradigm at its own recipe and best decoding.

blocks.en:
Generative retrieval (GR) maps a query directly to the identifier (docid)
of a relevant document. A docid is a short sequence of codes, and a
language model learns to generate it. Most GR models generate the docid
with an autoregressive (AR) decoder, one code at a time from left to right.
Recent work uses diffusion instead, in document
retrieval ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) and in
recommendation ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) . A
diffusion decoder starts from a fully masked docid and fills in its codes
over several steps. These works compare diffusion with AR, but they change
the identifier, the training settings and the decoding at the same time. A
difference in Hit@1 therefore cannot be credited to the generation
paradigm (AR or diffusion) alone.

blocks.en:
We separate these three factors ( Fig. 1 ). On NQ320K and
MS300K, we train four paradigms: AR, masked diffusion (MDLM), and block
diffusion with blocks of 4 or 8 codes (BD4, BD8). Each paradigm learns
several kinds of docids, from semantic to random. The semantic ones, RQ
and PQ, quantise a document embedding by residual or product
quantisation. Docid length, vocabulary and training budget are
fixed. We ask three questions. RQ1 : what does each paradigm learn? RQ2 : what does
diffusion generate, and which decoding finds the right document? RQ3 : does the identifier favour a paradigm?

blocks.en:
This paper makes three contributions. First, a controlled design crosses
paradigm, identifier and decoding on the same trained models. With it, we
show that decoding alone moves a diffusion model’s Hit@1 by 6.6 to 13.7 points.
Second, we turn one-pass scoring, a rule used by parallel-decoding
recommenders ( Hou et al., 2025 ) , into a decoding for diffusion retrievers: one forward pass on a fully masked docid scores every corpus
docid. It matches or beats generate-and-match, which generates a docid
and reranks the closest corpus docids, in 11 of 12 settings. Third, we list what
a paradigm comparison should report. We release the code, splits and
docids.

blocks.en: 2. Related Work
blocks.zh: 2. 相关工作

blocks.en:
Generative retrieval. DSI ( Tay et al., 2022 ) casts
retrieval as sequence-to-sequence generation. A T5 model maps a query to
the identifier of a relevant document, and beam search in a trie of
valid docids returns a ranking. Docids range from text, such as the
n-grams of SEAL ( Bevilacqua et al., 2022 ) , to semantic codes built from
document embeddings: hierarchical k-means in DSI and
NCI ( Wang et al., 2022 ) , product quantisation in
DDRO ( Mekonnen et al., 2025 ) , and residual quantisation in
TIGER ( Rajput et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2024 ) . Later work improves the codes, the training data and the
objective ( Sun et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2023 ; Zeng et al., 2024b ; Zhuang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Phatak et al., 2025 ; Askari et al., 2026 ) . All decode autoregressively. Studies
of docid construction show that the code changes the results with the
model held fixed ( Valeau et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . They keep
the paradigm fixed; we cross the identifier with the paradigm.

blocks.en:
Diffusion language models. Discrete
diffusion ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2024 ) corrupts a token sequence and
learns to undo the corruption. Masked diffusion
(MDLM ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) ) trains with a reweighted masked
language-modelling loss. It decodes by unmasking positions in any order.
Block diffusion (BD3-LM ( Arriola et al., 2025 ) ) decodes blocks from left
to right and the positions of a block in parallel. Comparisons with AR depend on
decoding. A reported diffusion advantage in language modelling came from
inaccurate sampling ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Diffusion models win on
per-token error but lose on whole-sequence error ( Feng et al., 2025 ) .
We therefore vary decoding on fixed checkpoints.

blocks.en:
Diffusion for generative retrieval. DiffuGR ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) retrieves
documents with diffusion models built on LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) and
Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , over RQ and text docids. It compares them with AR systems, each with its own docids,
training data and decoding. MaskGR ( Shah et al., 2025 ) compares masked
diffusion with an AR recommender. It tests random codes for diffusion
only. Diffusion recommenders ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2025 ; Mu et al., 2026 ) argue, with ablations, that independent, PQ-like codes suit parallel
decoders. EPIC ( Tran et al., 2026 ) scores complete items during
denoising, because committing tokens one at a time can drop the target.
In all of them, the code, the recipe and the decoder change together, so
a gain cannot be credited to the paradigm. We cross these factors and test
whether PQ codes favour parallel decoders.

blocks.en:
Decoding. PAG (Planning Ahead in Generative retrieval) scores
every document in one forward pass by summing the weights of a
second, lexical docid, and uses these scores as priors for AR beam
search ( Zeng et al., 2024a ) . Wu et al. show that AR GR scores a document
like multi-vector dense retrieval, with query vectors that depend on the
docid prefix ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . RPG scores every item by summing
per-digit log-probabilities from one pass of a parallel-prediction
model ( Hou et al., 2025 ) . One-pass scoring reads the query with
every docid level masked, and scores each docid by the probabilities of
its codes. We apply this rule to the denoiser of a trained diffusion model, with no
extra head, beam or denoising.

A generative retriever has three parts: the docid it generates, the
model that generates it (its paradigm, how it reads the query, how it is
trained), and the decoding that turns the model’s output into a ranked
list. We describe the options we test for each part.

Decoding. A trained model gives probabilities over codes, but

docid. So every beam ends on a docid, and beams are ranked by summed
log-probability. Greedy decoding keeps one beam, with or without the
trie; without it, a code that is no docid counts as a miss.

blocks.en:
AR leads or ties every learned-code cell ( Table 1 ), for
three possible reasons. First, AR predicts the first and last levels more accurately. On
NQ320K eval queries, from the query alone, AR predicts the first level
correctly 61% of the time, against 49–50% for diffusion with every
level masked on PQ (RQ: 70 against 59–60%); given the other 15 gold
levels, it predicts the last level correctly 79% of the time, against
67–78% (RQ: 82 against 54–58%). Second, AR is trained on all 17
outputs (16 levels and the end token) of every example and masked diffusion on about half, so a fixed
example budget favours AR. Third, AR’s backbone is larger and pretrained
differently: from random weights, AR scores 40.6 on NQ320K PQ, 8.2 points
below its Table 1 score and below MDLM’s 44.7.

lost signal for revealed levels to restore. On MS300K, only the two PQ losses exclude zero; on

At depth, the order reverses on NQ320K ( Fig. 2 b, c).
With one-pass scoring, MDLM ties AR’s beam at Hit@10 on PQ (63.5 against

not the cause. The depth gap matches what is proved for constrained beam
search ( Wu et al., 2025 ) : ranking prefixes by marginal probability
keeps Hit@1 but loses depth, whereas one-pass scoring scores every docid.

On NQ320K, the identifier does not favour diffusion over AR ( Table 1 ). If PQ-like codes suit parallel decoders
( Section 2 ), PQ’s lead should grow with the number of levels a model commits at once. On
NQ320K, PQ leads RQ by 3.4 points under AR, 3.6 under MDLM and 2.2 under
BD8. Under BD4 the two tie ( − 0.7 -0.7 ). Within diffusion, PQ’s lead grows
with the levels committed at once (BD4 − 0.7 -0.7 , BD8 2.2, MDLM 3.6), but AR,
one level at a time, matches MDLM (3.4). AR’s gap minus the mean
diffusion gap is + 1.7 +1.7 points with generate-and-match, inside our ± 2 \pm 2 -point
threshold, but 2.1 with one-pass scoring and 2.3 with chain-rule rescoring
( Fig. 4 b). At each model’s best decoding, it is 1.5, inside
the threshold. On MS300K, the point
estimates go the other way: AR’s beam favours PQ by 3.6 points, and
diffusion with chain-rule rescoring favours RQ by 3.6 to 6.7, an
interaction of 4.3 to 9.2 points across decodings, a hint against the
parallel-decoder hypothesis.

PQ’s lead depends on the decoding ( Fig. 4 b, c).
With one stochastic sample, PQ leads in all six diffusion cells, by 1.3 to

steadily (MDLM: 5.0, 3.0, 3.6, then 3.0 with one-pass scoring). On MS300K,
every diffusion model favours RQ with one-pass scoring and with chain-rule
rescoring. The rerank of the code-matching
candidates gains more on RQ in all four block-diffusion cells. A
one-sample comparison thus overstates PQ for diffusion.

blocks.en:
After a miss, the gold PQ document stays within reach; the gold
RQ one does not ( Fig. 4 a). We group misses by the first
level where the generation leaves the gold. When the generation leaves the
gold in its first four levels, the gold PQ document stays among the
candidates about 2.3 times as often as the gold RQ one; later, 1.3 to 1.4
times. The paradigms differ by only a few points. Recovery is thus a
property of the identifier, not of the paradigm. A near miss on PQ keeps
the other levels right, because they are independent. RQ’s later levels
are small residual corrections, and diffusion’s accuracy on them does not
rise with context ( Section 5.1 ). PQ leads although far more documents share a PQ code (1.4 against 0.1%). Scored on the document, its lead
shrinks but keeps its sign (AR: + 3.4 → + 1.9 +3.4\to+1.9 ).

With learned codes, the paradigm does not change where a miss
lands; the identifier, the corpus and the decoding do ( Fig. 5 ).
With PQ or RQ codes, one corpus and one decoding, the four paradigms share

points of diffusion generate-and-match. The paradigm changes how many
queries miss, not what a miss returns. Under RQ, one stochastic sample

one-pass scoring and chain-rule rescoring bring most of

are already topical for 46–49% on NQ320K and 63–66% on MS300K. Near-duplicates and near
codes stay at or below 10%. Random-code misses are mostly unrelated
(54–97%).

(AR’s beam, diffusion’s generate-and-match) reaches 62.6% Hit@1 on NQ320K,
against 48.8% for the best cell (MS300K: 49.1

diffusion with its own recipe ( Section 5.1 ). Second, decode with one-pass scoring. It matches or

blocks.en: 6. Limitations and Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6. 限制和结论

blocks.en:
Limitations. Four design choices bound our
results. The first is the models. The paradigms do not share a
backbone: AR’s T5 is pretrained on C4, about twenty times more text than
the diffusion models’ OpenWebText, and since AR trained from random
weights falls below MDLM ( Section 5.1 ), part of AR’s lead may
come from pretraining. Sizes are also only comparable, not matched
( Section 3 ), and we keep them below 500M parameters because a
retriever over a few hundred thousand documents should stay small; as
larger models may generate better, whether the ranking holds at scale
stays open. The second is training. AR’s recipe collapses diffusion
( Section 5.1 ), so each paradigm trains at its own, which leaves
recipe and paradigm partly entangled. The third is the data and the docids. RQ3 covers
one code shape and numeric docids, and RQ1 and RQ3 rest on NQ320K, because
on MS300K random codes do not converge within the budget and the identifier
gaps change sign across decodings. The last is the decoding. One-pass scoring is compared with
generative decodings only, not with a non-generative per-level
classifier, so how much of its gain needs diffusion is open, and its cost grows with
the corpus; why chain-rule rescoring costs MDLM 3.1 points on PQ is also
open.

blocks.en:
Conclusion. In this paper, we crossed paradigm, identifier and
decoding on the same trained models to ask why diffusion retrievers trail
autoregressive ones. First, diffusion models memorise like
AR ( Pradeep et al., 2023 ) , contrary to the intuition behind semantic
docids ( Tay et al., 2022 ; Rajput et al., 2023 ) :
on NQ320K, random codes without meaning keep 83–90% of RQ’s Hit@1 in
every paradigm, though on MS300K they do not converge within the budget (RQ1), and
the identifier separates AR from diffusion by 1.5 points at each model’s
best decoding on NQ320K, inside our threshold (RQ3). Second, decoding alone moves diffusion Hit@1 by 6.6 to 13.7
points. The generated docid is right for only 14–21% of NQ320K queries,
yet diffusion needs no iterative denoising to retrieve: one forward pass
on a fully masked docid matches or beats generate-and-match in 11 of 12
settings and, on NQ320K, reaches deeper than AR’s beam (RQ2). What remains is
AR’s lead in Hit@1, which on NQ320K comes from the model rather than its
beam and is entangled with pretraining. What reads as a paradigm gap is
thus partly a decoding gap: a paradigm comparison is fair only at each
paradigm’s own recipe and best decoding ( Section 5.5 ).
Our findings also open two directions. Since one forward pass yields an L × K L{\times}K table of code scores,
searching that table without scanning the corpus is a natural next step. Since every paradigm memorises, future work should test whether
training that reaches documents without a training query changes the
paradigm ranking.
